# Abnormalities of eyelid position

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Basics of ophthalmology > Abnormalities of eyelid position*

[Original Article Link](/library/lO0vsT)

---

## Summary

<u>Eyelid</u> closure allows for the distribution of tear fluid and glandular secretions, which protect the <u>cornea</u> and <u>conjunctiva</u> from <u>dehydration</u> and injury by foreign bodies. Pathological changes in <u>eyelid</u> position (i.e., <u>ptosis</u>, <u>ectropion</u>, <u>entropion</u>, <u>lagophthalmos</u>, and <u>blepharospasm</u>) prevent the complete protection of the <u>cornea</u> and <u>conjunctiva</u>, predisposing affected individuals to complications such as <u>keratitis</u>, <u>conjunctivitis</u>, and <u>corneal ulcers</u>. Treatment such as artificial tears and <u>eye</u> patches, as well as surgical procedures, can be used to help prevent such complications.




For other abnormalities of the eyelids, see “<u>Inflammation of the eyelids</u>” and “<u>Diseases of the lacrimal apparatus</u>.”

---

## Ptosis

* Definition: full or partial drooping or falling of one or both upper eyelids

* Etiology [[1]](/library/jmX_2A)[[2]](/library/PmXWfA)

* Congenital

* Myogenic

* Most common cause of congenital <u>ptosis</u>

* <u>Malformation</u> of the <u>levator palpebrae superioris muscle</u>

* Neurogenic: defective innervation of the upper <u>eyelid</u> (e.g., congenital third <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy, <u>synkinetic ptosis</u>, congenital <u>Horner syndrome</u>)

* Aponeurotic: defective insertion of the <u>aponeurosis</u> into the <u>anterior</u> surface of the eyelids

* <u>Blepharophimosis syndrome</u>

* Acquired

* Aponeurotic <u>ptosis</u>

* Most common cause of acquired <u>ptosis</u>

* Caused by dehiscence or stretching of the <u>aponeurosis</u> of the <u>levator palpebrae superioris muscle</u>

* More frequent in elderly individuals and in contact <u>lens</u> users

* Myogenic

* <u>Hypothyroid myopathy</u>

* <u>Mitochondrial myopathies</u> (e.g., <u>chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia</u>)

* <u>Myotonic syndromes</u> (e.g., <u>myotonic dystrophy type I</u>)

* Mechanical

* Excessive weight on the upper <u>eyelid</u> (e.g., <u>hemangioma</u>, <u>hematoma</u>, infections, tumors of the upper <u>eyelid</u>) prevents full opening of the <u>eye</u>.

* Causes <u>weakness</u> of the <u>levator palpebrae superioris muscle</u>

* <u>Oculomotor nerve palsy</u> 

* Due to neuropathy of internal neural fibers (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)

* Late manifestation of external compression (e.g., <u>posterior communicating artery</u> <u>aneurysm</u>, <u>uncal herniation</u>)

* <u>Ischemia</u> of the <u>oculomotor nerve</u>

* Neuromuscular disease (e.g., <u>myasthenia gravis</u>, <u>myotonia</u>, <u>botulism</u>)

* <u>Sympathetic</u> nerve injury

* Usually <u>Horner syndrome</u>

* Causes palsy or <u>weakness</u> of the <u>superior tarsal muscle</u>

* Traumatic

* Clinical features

* Congenital <u>ptosis</u>

* Unilateral

* Lid creases are absent or lower than normal.

* Acquired <u>ptosis</u>

* Can be unilateral or bilateral

* Associated with neurological symptoms (e.g., <u>pupillary</u> defects, <u>diplopia</u>) which vary depending on the underlying cause

* Diagnostics

* Family and <u>medical history</u>

* Clinical features (extraocular motility, <u>pupil</u> size, and reactivity)

* Treatment

* Treatment of the underlying condition

* Surgical

* Indications [[3]](/library/iMXJoA)

* Congenital <u>ptosis</u>

* Impaired <u>vision</u>

* <u>Eye</u> fatigue

* Difficulty reading

* Compensatory head alignment

* Procedures: will depend on the underlying etiology

* Blepharoplasty

* External levator advancement <u>surgery</u>

* Complications

* Congenital <u>ptosis</u>: <u>amblyopia</u>, <u>strabismus</u>

* Psychosocial problems

* Frontal <u>headaches</u>

* Decreased <u>visual field</u>

* <u>Lagophthalmos</u> (associated with corneal lesions)





> [!TIP]
> For patients with untreated congenital <u>ptosis</u>, <u>surgery</u> is indicated in an early stage due to the risk of developing <u>amblyopia</u>.

---

## Entropion

* Definition: inward folding of the <u>eyelid</u> margin

* Etiology

* Congenital <u>entropion</u>

* Lower <u>eyelid</u>

* Most common type of congenital <u>entropion</u>

* Due to increased direct mechanical pressure in utero or intrauterine tarsal deformity

* Upper <u>eyelid</u>: due to horizontal laxity of the <u>medial</u> or <u>lateral</u> canthal <u>tendons</u> or <u>facial nerve palsy</u>

* Involutional <u>entropion</u> 

* Most common type of <u>entropion</u>

* Frequency increases with age.

* Due to laxity of the <u>tarsal plates</u>, canthal <u>tendons</u>, and <u>eyelid</u> retractors

* <u>Spastic</u> <u>entropion</u>

* Usually accompanies involutional <u>entropion</u>

* An exaggerated contraction of the orbicularis muscle, leading to the preseptal part of the muscle to override the <u>tarsal plate</u>

* Due to preexisting lower <u>eyelid</u> laxity or ocular irritation (e.g., due to infection, inflammation, trauma)

* Cicatricial <u>entropion</u>

* Vertical tarsoconjunctival <u>contracture</u> and <u>internal rotation</u> of the <u>eyelid</u> margin

* Due to scarring (e.g., due to <u>trachoma</u>, ocular pemphigoid, infection, trauma)  [[7]](/library/SMXyLA)

* Clinical features

* Congenital <u>entropion</u>: usually asymptomatic

* Can manifest with <u>photosensitivity</u>, <u>blepharospasm</u>, and/or infrequent <u>eye</u> opening

* Manifestation depends on the clinical malposition of the eyelids

* Acquired <u>entropion</u>

* <u>Trichiasis</u>

* Recurrent <u>blepharospasm</u>

* Ocular <u>pruritus</u>

* <u>Ciliary injection</u> or <u>conjunctival injection</u>

* Foreign body sensation in the <u>eye</u>

* <u>Epiphora</u>

* <u>Hemifacial spasms</u> (seen in <u>spastic</u> <u>entropion</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Clinical features

* Complete <u>eye examination</u>

* <u>Exophthalmopathy</u>: in cases of involutional <u>entropion</u> to rule out <u>exophthalmos</u>

* Treatment [[8]](/library/RMXloA)

* Treatment of the underlying condition

* Congenital <u>entropion</u> typically does not require treatment and often involutes spontaneously.

* Palliative

* Artificial tears and ointments

* Soft contact lenses: protect the <u>cornea</u> from external injury

* <u>Skin</u> tape: used to hold the lid in place

* Cyanoacrylate liquid bandage: used to evert the lid

* <u>Botulinum toxin</u> application on the orbicularis muscle: in case of <u>spastic</u> <u>entropion</u>

* Removal of the eyelashes: in case of <u>trichiasis</u>

* Surgical

* Definitive treatment

* Indications [[8]](/library/RMXloA)

* Recurrent <u>erosions</u>

* Recurrent infections

* Uncontrolled <u>eye</u> inflammation

* Procedure: Suture <u>eversion</u> of the lid.

* Complications

* <u>Trichiasis</u>

* <u>Amblyopia</u> with possible <u>vision loss</u>

* <u>Conjunctival</u> and corneal lesions (e.g., corneal thinning, scarring, <u>ulcers</u>)
